claims.text: Homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles form when the effective atomic-mobility period immediately after reduction is sufficiently short to kinetically freeze the mixture.
The starting material is a solid or quasi-solid mixture containing precursors for at least five noble metals.
Heating and cooling rates can be used to modulate the effective mobility time while other synthesis parameters remain constant.
The relevant synthesis regime is rapid, high-temperature reduction lasting milliseconds to seconds.
The constituent precursors are reduced nearly simultaneously.
The extent of atomic mobility determines whether the atoms remain in a homogeneous alloy or form separated phases.
Minimizing the post-reduction mobility period prevents significant atomic diffusion.
Limited mobility promotes a stochastic formation process that locks in a uniform random alloy composition.
An extended mobility period lets atoms rearrange according to thermodynamic preferences, causing phase separation and elemental segregation.
Increasing the effective mobility time relative to an ultra-rapid baseline will increase measurable phase separation or elemental segregation.
Further shortening the mobility period will consistently produce homogeneous HEA nanoparticles.
Further shortening the mobility period will produce high-surface-area nanoparticles.
An ultra-rapid heating and quenching protocol such as carbothermal shock is known to yield predominantly single-phase, homogeneous HEA nanoparticles.
The ultra-rapid baseline produces homogeneity by suppressing atomic diffusion.
The proposed mobility-controlled mechanism should apply to noble metal systems containing five or more elements prepared from solid or mixed precursors.
The mechanism may not apply to lower-temperature or solution-based syntheses because atomic mobility is inherently higher there.
The mobility-time threshold for switching between homogeneous alloying and segregation depends on the elemental combination and precursor chemistry.
